# rkyv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rkyv/^0.8.8/

## Expand description

rkyv is a zero-copy deserialization framework for Rust.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

rkyv uses Rust’s powerful trait system to serialize data without reflection. Many zero-copy deserialization frameworks use external schemas and heavily restrict the available data types. By contrast, rkyv allows all serialized types to be defined in code and can serialize a wide variety of types that other frameworks cannot.

rkyv scales to highly-capable as well as highly-restricted environments. Not only does rkyv support “no-std” builds for targets without a standard library implementation, it also supports “no-alloc” builds for targets where allocations cannot be made.

rkyv supports limited in-place data mutation, and so can access and update data without ever deserializing back to native types. When rkyv’s in-place mutation is too limited, rkyv also provides ergonomic and performant deserialization back into native types.

rkyv prioritizes performance, and is one of the fastest serialization frameworks available. All of rkyv’s features can be individually enabled and disabled, so you only pay for what you use. Additionally, all of rkyv’s zero-copy types are designed to have little to no overhead. In most cases, rkyv’s types will have exactly the same performance as native types.

See the [rkyv book](https://rkyv.org) for guide-level documentation.
See [the examples directory](https://github.com/rkyv/rkyv/tree/main/rkyv/examples) for usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#components)Components

rkyv has [a hash map implementation](https://docs.rs/collections/swiss_table/map/struct.ArchivedHashMap.html) that is built for zero-copy
deserialization, with the same lookup and iteration performance as the
standard library hash maps. The hash map implementation is based on
[Swiss Tables](https://abseil.io/about/design/swisstables) and uses a target-independent version of FxHash to ensure
that all targets compute the same hashes.

It also has [a B-tree implementation](https://docs.rs/collections/btree_map/struct.ArchivedBTreeMap.html) that has the same performance
characteristics as the standard library B-tree maps. Its compact
representation and localized data storage is best-suited for very large
amounts of data.

rkyv supports [shared pointers](https://docs.rs/rc/index.html) by default, and is able to serialize and
deserialize them without duplicating the underlying data. Shared pointers
which point to the same data when serialized will still point to the same
data when deserialized. By default, rkyv only supports non-cyclic data
structures.

Alongside its [unchecked API](https://docs.rs/fn.access_unchecked.html), rkyv also provides optional [validation](https://docs.rs/fn.access.html) so
you can ensure safety and data integrity at the cost of some overhead.
Because checking serialized data can generally be done without allocations,
the cost of checking and zero-copy access can be much lower than that of
traditional deserialization.

rkyv is trait-oriented from top to bottom, and is made to be extended with custom and specialized types. Serialization, deserialization, and validation traits all accept generic context types, making it easy to add new capabilities without degrading ergonomics.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

rkyv has several feature flags which can be used to modify its behavior. By
default, rkyv enables the `std`, `alloc`, and `bytecheck` features.

[§](https://docs.rs#format-control)Format control

These features control how rkyv formats its serialized data. Enabling and disabling these features may change rkyv’s serialized format, and as such can cause previously-serialized data to become unreadable. Enabling format control features that are not the default should be considered a breaking change to rkyv’s serialized format.

Binaries should consider explicitly choosing format control options from the start, even though doing so is not required. This ensures that developers stay informed about the specific choices being made, and prevents any unexpected compatibility issues with libraries they depend on.

Libraries should avoid enabling format control features unless they intend to only support rkyv when those specific format control features are enabled. In general, libraries should be able to support all format control options if they use rkyv’s exported types and aliases.

[§](https://docs.rs#endianness)Endianness

If an endianness feature is not enabled, rkyv will use little-endian byte ordering by default.

- `little_endian`: Forces data serialization to use little-endian byte ordering. This optimizes serialized data for little-endian architectures.
- `big_endian`: Forces data serialization to use big-endian byte ordering. This optimizes serialized data for big-endian architectures.

[§](https://docs.rs#alignment)Alignment

If an alignment feature is not enabled, rkyv will use aligned primitives by default.

- `aligned`: Forces data serialization to use aligned primitives. This adds alignment requirements for accessing data and prevents rkyv from working with unaligned data.
- `unaligned`: Forces data serialization to use unaligned primitives. This removes alignment requirements for accessing data and allows rkyv to work with unaligned data more easily.

[§](https://docs.rs#pointer-width)Pointer width

If a pointer width feature is not enabled, rkyv will serialize `isize` and
`usize` as 32-bit integers by default.

- `pointer_width_16`: Serializes- `isize`and- `usize`as 16-bit integers. This is intended to be used only for small data sizes and may not handle large amounts of data.
- `pointer_width_32`: Serializes- `isize`and- `usize`as 32-bit integers. This is a good choice for most data, and balances the storage overhead with support for large data sizes.
- `pointer_width_64`: Serializes- `isize`and- `usize`as 64-bit integers. This is intended to be used only for extremely large data sizes and may cause unnecessary data bloat for smaller amounts of data.

[§](https://docs.rs#functionality)Functionality

These features enable more built-in functionality and provide more powerful and ergonomic APIs. Enabling and disabling these features does not change rkyv’s serialized format.

- `alloc`: Enables support for the- `alloc`crate. Enabled by default.
- `std`: Enables standard library support. Enabled by default.
- `bytecheck`: Enables data validation through- `bytecheck`. Enabled by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#crates)Crates

rkyv provides integrations for some common crates by default. In the future, crates should depend on rkyv and provide their own integration. Enabling and disabling these features does not change rkyv’s serialized format.

- `arrayvec-0_7`
- `bytes-1`
- `hashbrown-0_14`
- `hashbrown-0_15`
- `hashbrown-0_16`
- `hashbrown-0_17`
- `indexmap-2`
- `smallvec-1`
- `smol_str-0_2`
- `smol_str-0_3`
- `thin-vec-0_2`
- `tinyvec-1`
- `triomphe-0_1`
- `uuid-1`

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

Serialized data can be accessed later as long as:

- The underlying schema has not changed
- The serialized format has not been changed by format control features
- The data was serialized by a semver-compatible version of rkyv

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |

# calib_targets_charuco - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets-charuco/0.10.0/calib_targets_charuco/

## Expand description

ChArUco-related utilities.

Current focus:

- chessboard detection from ChESS corners,
- per-cell marker decoding (no full-image warp by default),
- alignment to a known board definition and corner ID assignment.

Marker dictionaries and decoding live in `calib-targets-aruco`.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
use calib_targets_charuco::{
    builtins, CharucoBoardSpec, CharucoDetector, CharucoParams, ChessCorner,
    GrayImageView, MarkerLayout,
};
let board = CharucoBoardSpec::new(5, 7, 1.0, 0.7, builtins::DICT_4X4_50)
    .with_marker_layout(MarkerLayout::OpenCvCharuco);
let params = CharucoParams::for_board(&board);
let detector = CharucoDetector::new(params)?;
let pixels = vec![0u8; 32 * 32];
let view = GrayImageView {
    width: 32,
    height: 32,
    data: &pixels,
};
let corners: Vec<ChessCorner> = Vec::new();
let _ = detector.detect(&view, &corners)?;
```

# calib_targets_aruco - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets-aruco/0.10.0/calib_targets_aruco/

## Expand description

ArUco/AprilTag marker dictionaries and decoding utilities.

This crate focuses on:

- embedded built-in dictionaries (compiled into the binary),
- matching observed marker codes against those dictionaries,
- decoding markers either from rectified grids or from per-cell image quads.

It does **not** perform quad detection. Instead, it expects a grid model
(for example from `calib-targets-chessboard`) or explicit cell corners.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
use calib_targets_aruco::{
    builtins, scan_decode_markers, GrayImageView, Matcher, ScanDecodeConfig,
};
let dict = builtins::builtin_dictionary("DICT_4X4_50").expect("dict");
let matcher = Matcher::new(dict, 1);
let pixels = vec![0u8; 16 * 16];
let view = GrayImageView {
    width: 16,
    height: 16,
    data: &pixels,
};
let scan_cfg = ScanDecodeConfig::default();
let markers = scan_decode_markers(&view, 4, 4, 4.0, &scan_cfg, &matcher);
println!("markers: {}", markers.len());
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [builtins](https://docs.rs/builtins/index.html)
- Embedded built-in dictionaries.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- Optional overrides for marker scanning and matching.
- [Cell](https://docs.rs/struct.CellSamples.html)- Samples
- Rectified per-cell intensity samples suitable for custom match scoring.
- [Dictionary](https://docs.rs/struct.Dictionary.html)
- A fixed ArUco/AprilTag-style dictionary.
- [Gray](https://docs.rs/struct.GrayImageView.html)- Image - View
- Borrowed view over an 8-bit grayscale image.
- [Marker](https://docs.rs/struct.MarkerCell.html)- Cell
- One square cell with its image-space corners.
- [Marker](https://docs.rs/struct.MarkerDetection.html)- Detection
- One decoded marker detection.
- [Match](https://docs.rs/struct.Match.html)
- A dictionary match for an observed marker code.
- [Matcher](https://docs.rs/struct.Matcher.html)
- Matcher for a fixed dictionary.
- [Scan](https://docs.rs/struct.ScanDecodeConfig.html)- Decode - Config
- Decoder configuration for scanning markers.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_marker_in_cell.html)- marker_ - in_ - cell
- Decode a single marker from one square cell in image space.
- [rotate_](https://docs.rs/fn.rotate_code_u64.html)- code_ - u64
- Rotate a code stored in row-major bits: `idx = y * N + x`.
- [sample_](https://docs.rs/fn.sample_cell.html)- cell
- Sample a rectified per-cell intensity grid from an image using a cell quad, without decoding any marker id.

# calib_targets_chessboard - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets-chessboard/0.10.0/calib_targets_chessboard/

## Expand description

Invariant-first chessboard detector.

Takes a slice of [ChESS](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/research/rainbow/projects/chess/)
X-junction corners and returns an integer-labelled chessboard grid. The
crate’s only output contract is: *every labelled corner has been proven
to sit at a real grid intersection.* Missing corners are acceptable;
wrong corners are not.

**High detection rate on our private regression set with zero wrong
 (i, j) labels** (non-negligible lens distortion and motion blur).

Algorithm reference: see `book/src/chessboard.md`.

[§](https://docs.rs#pipeline)Pipeline

The detector builds its `(i, j)` labelling with the **topological** grid
finder in [ projective_grid](https://docs.rs/projective-grid/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/projective_grid/index.html) (a Delaunay triangulation + an axis-driven
cell test), then runs a chessboard-specific recovery + precision pass over
the labelled components:

| Stage | Name | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `prefilter` | Drop corners failing strength / fit-quality / axes-validity gates. |
| 2 | `cluster_axes` | Recover the two global grid-direction centres `{Θ₀, Θ₁}`via histogram + 2-means; label each corner as canonical or swapped. |
| 3 | `topological_grid` | Delaunay + axis-driven cell test → connected labelled `(i, j)`components ().`projective_grid::detect_grid_all` |
| 4 | `recover_components` | Per-component recall boosters (interior gap fill + line extrapolation with a directional edge scale) + shared component merge. |
| 5 | `final_geometry_check` | Mandatory precision gate: line collinearity + local-H residual + direct wrong-label check + largest cardinal component. Can only drop corners; never adds. |
| 6 | `output` | Labelled grid → canonicalised, non-negative-rebased .`ChessboardDetection` |

Each stage is its own module or function; see the submodules.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
use calib_targets_chessboard::{ChessCorner, Detector, DetectorParams};
use calib_targets_core::AxisEstimate;
use nalgebra::Point2;
// A synthetic 7×7 chessboard corner cloud at 20 px pitch. Adjacent
// corners carry opposite axis-slot orderings (the parity invariant).
let mut corners: Vec<ChessCorner> = Vec::new();
for j in 0..7 {
    for i in 0..7 {
        let swapped = (i + j) % 2 == 1;
        let (a0, a1) = if swapped {
            (std::f32::consts::FRAC_PI_2, 0.0)
        } else {
            (0.0, std::f32::consts::FRAC_PI_2)
        };
        corners.push(ChessCorner {
            position: Point2::new(i as f32 * 20.0 + 50.0, j as f32 * 20.0 + 50.0),
            axes: [
                AxisEstimate { angle: a0, sigma: 0.01 },
                AxisEstimate { angle: a1, sigma: 0.01 },
            ],
            contrast: 10.0,
            fit_rms: 1.0,
            // Above the default `min_corner_strength` floor (33.0).
            strength: 100.0,
        });
    }
}
let det = Detector::new(DetectorParams::default()).expect("default params are valid");
let detection = det.detect(&corners).expect("clean 7×7 grid detects");
assert_eq!(detection.corners.len(), 49);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rectification-helpers)Rectification helpers

Two rectifiers are exposed: [ rectify_from_chessboard_result](https://docs.rs/fn.rectify_from_chessboard_result.html)
(

[) and](https://docs.rs/struct.RectifiedBoardView.html)

`RectifiedBoardView`[(](https://docs.rs/fn.rectify_mesh_from_grid.html)

`rectify_mesh_from_grid`[). The former takes a](https://docs.rs/struct.RectifiedMeshView.html)

`RectifiedMeshView`[directly; the latter is pattern-agnostic and takes a](https://docs.rs/struct.ChessboardDetection.html)

`ChessboardDetection``&[LabeledCorner]` plus an inlier index list. Both produce a
rectified view and can be used with any consistent `(i, j)`
labelling.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Advanced](https://docs.rs/struct.AdvancedTuning.html)- Tuning
- Advanced, **unstable**per-stage tuning knobs for the chessboard detector.
- [Chess](https://docs.rs/struct.ChessCorner.html)- Corner
- Canonical 2D corner consumed by the chessboard detector.
- [Chessboard](https://docs.rs/struct.ChessboardCorner.html)- Corner
- A single labelled chessboard corner.
- [Chessboard](https://docs.rs/struct.ChessboardDetection.html)- Detection
- Result of chessboard detection: the labelled corner set.
- [Detector](https://docs.rs/struct.Detector.html)
- Top-level detector.
- [Detector](https://docs.rs/struct.DetectorParams.html)- Params
- Top-level detector configuration.
- [Rectified](https://docs.rs/struct.RectifiedBoardView.html)- Board - View
- A rectified, fronto-parallel view of a detected chessboard.
- [Rectified](https://docs.rs/struct.RectifiedMeshView.html)- Mesh - View

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [detect_](https://docs.rs/fn.detect_all_topological.html)- all_ - topological
- Run the topological pipeline and return one `ChessboardDetection`
- [rectify_](https://docs.rs/fn.rectify_from_chessboard_result.html)- from_ - chessboard_ - result

- [trace_](https://docs.rs/fn.trace_topological.html)- topological
- Run the same topological input adaptation as `detect_all_topological`

# calib_targets_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets-core/0.10.0/calib_targets_core/

## Expand description

Core types and utilities for calibration target detection.

This crate is intentionally small and purely geometric. It does *not*
depend on any concrete corner detector implementation or image type, but it
owns the shared detector configuration contracts used across the workspace.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
use calib_targets_core::{LabeledCorner, TargetDetection, TargetKind};
use nalgebra::Point2;
let corner = LabeledCorner::new(Point2::new(12.0, 8.0), 0.9);
let detection = TargetDetection::new(TargetKind::Chessboard, vec![corner]);
println!("{}", detection.corners.len());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#includes)Includes

- Homography estimation and warping helpers.
- Lightweight grayscale image views and sampling.
- Grid alignment and target detection types.

# projective_grid - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/projective-grid/0.10.0/projective_grid/

## Expand description

Target-agnostic projective grid recovery primitives.

This crate is intentionally small at the public boundary. It models two lattice families, two tasks, and explicit evidence shapes. Target-specific identifiers and detector classes belong in caller crates and should be converted into generic point features or coordinate hypotheses before entering this crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#design-references)Design references

The crate is organised around three orthogonal axes — lattice family,
recovery strategy, and input-feature kind. The architecture and the
orientation-as-an-optional-cue model are documented under `docs/` in the
crate source tree:

- `docs/DESIGN.md`— the three design axes, the shared pipeline back-half, and how the lattice family extends to hex.
- `docs/ORIENTATION.md`— where each strategy consumes per-corner orientation and how each can run orientation-free (the dot-grid path).

The per-strategy stage maps live in `docs/algorithms/topological-grid-detection.md`
(repo root) and `calib-targets-chessboard/docs/PIPELINE.md`.

[§](https://docs.rs#two-public-tiers)Two public tiers

The crate ships an intentional two-tier public API. Both tiers are supported; they differ in audience and in how fast the surface is allowed to move.

[§](https://docs.rs#stable-tier--the-facade-ordinary-users)Stable tier — the facade (ordinary users)

The items re-exported at the crate root are the supported surface for an
ordinary caller who wants to *detect a grid* and read the labels back:

- the entry points `detect_grid``detect_grid_all``check_consistency`
- the request types `Evidence``DetectionParams``DetectionRequest``ConsistencyParams``ConsistencyRequest`
- the result types `GridSolution``LabelledGrid``DetectionReport`
- the lattice model `Lattice``LatticeKind``Coord``PointFeature``OrientedFeature``LocalAxis`
- the orientation-synthesis helpers (`synthesize_oriented2``cluster_axes``AxisClusterCenters``AxisAssignment`

This tier carries normal semver guarantees: breaking changes here go through the usual deprecation cycle.

[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-tier--the-composition-api-build-your-own-detector)Advanced tier — the composition API (build your own detector)

[ shared](https://docs.rs/shared/index.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/topological/index.html)

`topological`[,](https://docs.rs/lattice/index.html)

`lattice`[, and](https://docs.rs/orient/index.html)

`orient`[expose the assembly engine the facade is built from, as a deliberate](https://docs.rs/cluster/index.html)

`cluster`**composition API**. It exists so a consumer with its own per-pattern invariants — the in-workspace chessboard detector is the reference example, but the contract is written for external consumers too — can drive the same grid-growth and recovery machinery under its own policy instead of going through the one-size-fits-all facade. This is intended product, not a private engine that merely happens to be

`pub`.The composition contract — what a consumer supplies and what the engine guarantees in return:

- **You supply a**This is the seam between the geometry-only growth machinery and your pattern’s rules. The policy answers four questions per candidate —- `shared::grow::SquareAttachPolicy`- `is_eligible`,- `required_label_at`,- `accept_candidate`,- `edge_ok`— letting you veto an attachment that is geometrically plausible but illegal for your pattern (e.g. a chessboard’s alternating-colour parity, or a per-corner blacklist). The engine never relabels behind your back: every attachment it proposes has already passed your policy.
- **You drive the growth / recovery engine.**The geometry-only primitives live under- `shared`- `shared::grow`- `shared::fill`- `shared::extension`- `shared::grow_extend`- `shared::recovery_schedule`- `RecoverySchedule`- `RecoveryParams`
- **You compose the shared back-half.**After your front-half has built integer-labelled components, the lattice-parameterised back-half reunites them with local geometry only (- `shared::merge`- `shared::validate`- `Lattice`
- **The guarantees.**Every stage is- *drop-only*with respect to labels: a corner whose geometry does not cohere is removed, never relabelled. The precision contract of the facade —- **zero wrong**, misses acceptable — therefore holds for a consumer that composes the engine under its own policy, because the policy gates and the validate/drop filters run on every attachment exactly as they do on the facade path. Returned components are rebased so the labelled bounding-box minimum is- `(i, j)`labels- `(0, 0)`; quad / homography corner order is TL, TR, BR, BL.

**Stability of the advanced tier.** This surface is *advanced, and may
evolve*: its shape tracks the engine’s internal structure, so an item may
change between minor releases when the engine is refactored. That is a
deliberate product choice — the tier trades a slower-moving contract for
direct access to the engine — not a disclaimer that it is really private.
If you only need to detect a grid, depend on the facade; reach for the
composition tier when you are building a *new kind of detector* on top of
the engine. Engine items with no external consumer stay `pub(crate)`, so
the advanced surface is kept no wider than what a consumer actually
composes.

[§](https://docs.rs#core-vs-extended-surface)Core vs. extended surface

Orthogonal to the stable/advanced split is a second distinction worth making explicit, because the two halves are exercised very differently in practice:

- **Core path (exercised in production).**The square lattice (- `LatticeKind::Square`- `Evidence::Oriented2`
- **Extended path (library-only breadth).**The hexagonal lattice (- `Hex`- `topological`- `D6_TRANSFORMS`- `orient`- `shared::recovery_schedule`- `Evidence::Positions`- `Evidence::Oriented1`- `docs/DESIGN.md`for the full core-vs-extended map.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [check](https://docs.rs/check/index.html)
- Consistency-check task facade.
- [cluster](https://docs.rs/cluster/index.html)
- Global grid-direction recovery from per-feature dual-axis estimates.
- [detect](https://docs.rs/detect/index.html)
- Detection task facade.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Error types for grid tasks.
- [feature](https://docs.rs/feature/index.html)
- Generic feature evidence consumed by grid tasks.
- [float](https://docs.rs/float/index.html)
- Sealed `Float`
- [geometry](https://docs.rs/geometry/index.html)
- Geometry helpers shared by grid tasks.
- [lattice](https://docs.rs/lattice/index.html)
- Lattice-family axis: the parameter that the strategies and the shared back-half are written against, rather than a copy per family.
- [orient](https://docs.rs/orient/index.html)
- Local lattice-orientation synthesis from point positions alone.
- [result](https://docs.rs/result/index.html)
- Shared output types for detection and consistency tasks.
- [shared](https://docs.rs/shared/index.html)
- Shared detection back-half plus the geometry-only grid-growth engine.
- [topological](https://docs.rs/topological/index.html)
- Axis-driven topological grid finder (Shu/Brunton/Fiala 2009) for the
`(LatticeKind::Square, Evidence::Oriented2)`slot.

Shared OAuth primitives used by provider crates that implement OAuth-based auth (Codex, Google). API-key backends bypass this module.

Provider-specific endpoints, device-code flows, PKCE helpers, and
refresh logic live in each provider crate under `oauth.rs`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [extract_](https://docs.rs/fn.extract_query_param.html)- query_ - param
- Extract the value of a given query parameter from a URL or raw
query-string. Returns `None`if the key is absent.
- [generate_](https://docs.rs/fn.generate_pkce.html)- pkce
- Generate a PKCE code verifier and challenge pair. PKCE verifier is 32 bytes of OS entropy (via two UUID v4s) base64url-encoded; the challenge is its SHA-256 base64url-encoded.

- [percent_](https://docs.rs/fn.percent_decode.html)- decode
- Percent-decode a query-string value (handles `+`→ space).

- Form-urlencoded body encoder for OAuth token endpoints.
- [urlencoded](https://docs.rs/fn.urlencoded.html)

# solana_log_parser - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-log-parser/0.1.0/solana_log_parser/

## Expand description

A parser for Solana transaction logs.

Solana runtime logs are a flat, ordered sequence of strings describing
program invocations, their nested inner instructions, and any messages
programs emit along the way (`msg!`, compute unit reports, return data,
etc). This crate turns that flat list into a tree of [ InstructionCall](https://docs.rs/struct.InstructionCall.html)s
that mirrors the actual call structure, so callers can walk invocations
and their children without re-parsing stack height markers themselves.

This crate is `no_std` (with `alloc`) so it can be used in constrained
environments such as on-chain programs or WASM.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let logs: Vec<String> = /* raw transaction logs */;
let instructions = Parser::parse(&logs)?;
for top_level in &instructions {
    for call in top_level.iter() {
        println!("{} at depth {}", call.program_id, call.stack_height);
    }
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Instruction](https://docs.rs/struct.InstructionCall.html)- Call
- A single program invocation, including any nested inner instructions it made and the logs it emitted.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineParser.html)- Parser
- Parses individual log lines that are known to belong to a specific program.
- [Parser](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html)
- Entry point for parsing raw transaction logs into a tree of
`InstructionCall`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.ErrorStatus.html)- Status
- Like `Status`
- [Line](https://docs.rs/enum.Line.html)
- The parsed classification of a single raw log line.
- [Log](https://docs.rs/enum.Log.html)
- One entry in an `InstructionCall`
- [LogHint](https://docs.rs/enum.LogHint.html)
- Categorizes what kind of program log a `Log::Program``Program log:`,`Program consumed`).
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/enum.ParseError.html)- Error
- Errors that can occur while parsing transaction logs.
- [Status](https://docs.rs/enum.Status.html)
- The outcome of a completed program invocation.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [parse](https://docs.rs/fn.parse.html)
- Parses a full list of transaction log lines into the top-level instructions (and their nested invocations) they describe.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_line.html)- line
- Classifies a single raw log line into a `Line`

# opys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/opys/0.10.1/opys/

## Expand description

opys — a file-based inventory of typed markdown documents: one markdown file
per document, with YAML frontmatter, stable IDs, tags, configurable types,
test plans, and a `verify` gate for CI.

The binary is a thin wrapper around [ run](https://docs.rs/fn.run.html). The modules are public so the
crate can be used as a library.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use error::`- [OpysError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.OpysError.html);
- `pub use error::`- [Result](https://docs.rs/error/type.Result.html);
- `pub use frontmatter::`- [Frontmatter](https://docs.rs/frontmatter/struct.Frontmatter.html);
- `pub use project::`- [Project](https://docs.rs/project/struct.Project.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [body](https://docs.rs/body/index.html)
- Parsing of the markdown body: title, sections, and checklist items.
- [cli](https://docs.rs/cli/index.html)
- Command-line interface (clap derive).
- [commands](https://docs.rs/commands/index.html)
- Subcommand implementations. Each `run`takes the invocation`Ctx`
- [config](https://docs.rs/config/index.html)
- Shared field-spec types used by the universal config (`opys.toml`). See`crate::project_config`
- [doc](https://docs.rs/doc/index.html)
- A single inventory document in memory — the unified representation of every
configured type. This collapses the former `Feature`and`WorkItem`, which were identical`{path, frontmatter, body, title}`structs; a doc’s*type*is derived from its ID prefix via the config, not stored here.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- [file_](https://docs.rs/file_refs/index.html)- refs
- Scan source files for textual references to document ids.
- [frontmatter](https://docs.rs/frontmatter/index.html)
- Frontmatter parsing and canonical serialization.
- [links](https://docs.rs/links/index.html)
- Cross-reference auto-sync: keep every doc’s `references`map bidirectional and title-fresh, and rewrite bare`FEAT-XXXX`/`WI-XXXX`mentions in body prose into readable markdown links. Run by`sync`after every mutating command.
- [mdprism](https://docs.rs/mdprism/index.html)
- mdprism — markdown ⇄ data, via a template
- [palette](https://docs.rs/palette/index.html)
- Configurable presentation rules for the TUI (`[palette]`in opys.toml).
- [project](https://docs.rs/project/index.html)
- The project: `opys.toml`at the project root (found by searching upward), plus the inventory base it points at (default`opys/`, holding the document files and`_retired.txt`).
- [project_](https://docs.rs/project_config/index.html)- config
- The universal typed-document config (`opys.toml`) — the sole source of truth for the engine.
- [refs](https://docs.rs/refs/index.html)
- The uniform `references`field: an ID->title map linking a feature or work item to other features and work items.
- [rules](https://docs.rs/rules/index.html)
- The conditional validation-rules engine for the universal config.
- [templates](https://docs.rs/templates/index.html)
- String templates emitted by `opys init`and`opys agent-rules`.
- [tui](https://docs.rs/tui/index.html)
- Interactive terminal UI for opys — a live board over the inventory that updates as documents change on disk.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Ctx](https://docs.rs/struct.Ctx.html)
- Shared invocation context: where the inventory lives and global flags.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [run](https://docs.rs/fn.run.html)
- Execute a parsed CLI invocation, returning the process exit code.

# eql_bindings - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/eql-bindings/0.2.0/eql_bindings/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#eql-bindings--canonical-eql-payload-types)eql-bindings — canonical EQL payload types

One Rust definition per EQL payload shape — the single source of truth
for every tool that produces or consumes EQL payloads
(`cipherstash-client`, `protect-ffi`, CipherStash Proxy). TypeScript
bindings (`ts-rs`) and JSON Schemas (`schemars`) are generated from
these definitions — run `cargo test`, see `bindings/v3/` and
`schema/v3/`. The Rust types are the contract.

ts-rs rule for the generated flat-scalar payload structs (learned from the
original spike): ts-rs silently drops a serde attribute it cannot parse, so
keep field-level serde attributes out of generated scalar structs — which
the flat-scalar wire rule below already demands. The hand-written SteVec
`jsonb` structs are the exception: they deliberately use serde `flatten`,
`default`, and `skip_serializing_if` because that wire shape is not
derivable from the scalar catalog.

The [ v3](https://docs.rs/v3/index.html) module holds the

`eql_v3` encrypted-domain types: one struct
per SQL domain (`eql_v3.int4_eq`, `eql_v3.text_match`, …),
*capability-encoded*— index terms are required fields, never

`Option`.
The generated flat-scalar payload structs mirror the scalar subset of
`eql-domains::CATALOG` 1:1, enforced by `tests/catalog_parity.rs`; the
hand-written SteVec `jsonb` structs are still listed in the generated
inventory so the full `v3::all()` surface remains catalog-ordered.Wire rule: **field names ARE wire names** — no `#[serde(rename)]`
anywhere. The struct definition reads exactly like the JSON payload.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Identifier](https://docs.rs/struct.Identifier.html)
- Table + column identifier — wire shape `{"t": "...", "c": "..."}`.
- [Schema](https://docs.rs/struct.SchemaVersion.html)- Version
- The envelope version field (`v`) — always exactly`EQL_SCHEMA_VERSION`

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [EQL_](https://docs.rs/constant.EQL_SCHEMA_VERSION.html)- SCHEMA_ - VERSION
- EQL wire-format version. Hard-coded to `3`for every payload in the`v3``VALUE->>'v' = '3'`. (The legacy`eql_v2`wire stays`v: 2`— see`docs/reference/schema/eql-payload-v2.*.schema.json`.)

---

## Crate sc_lint_attributes

## [sc_lint_attributes](../sc_lint_attributes/index.html)0.4.0

  * [All Items](all.html)

# rkyv_util::owned - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rkyv_util/0.1.0-alpha.1/rkyv_util/owned/index.html

## Expand description

Enables us to pass around owned archive types.

This can be useful in many situations. For instance, suppose we want to pass Archives around in channels but we do not want to deal with complicated lifetimes.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Owned](https://docs.rs/struct.OwnedArchive.html)- Archive
- An owned archive type.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Stable](https://docs.rs/trait.StableBytes.html)- Bytes
- A contract guaranteeing that bytes should originate from the same source between accesses.
- [Stable](https://docs.rs/trait.StableBytesMut.html)- Bytes - Mut
- A contract guaranteeing that bytes should originate from the same source between acceses.

# bytecheck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytecheck/^0.8/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#bytecheck)bytecheck

bytecheck is a memory validation framework for Rust.

For some types, creating an invalid value immediately results in undefined behavior. This can cause some issues when trying to validate potentially invalid bytes, as just casting the bytes to your type can technically cause errors. This makes it difficult to write validation routines, because until you’re certain that the bytes represent valid values you cannot cast them.

bytecheck provides a framework for performing these byte-level validations and implements checks for basic types along with a derive macro to implement validation for custom structs and enums.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

[ CheckBytes](https://docs.rs/trait.CheckBytes.html) is at the heart of bytecheck, and does the heavy lifting of
verifying that some bytes represent a valid type. Implementing it can be
done manually or automatically with the

[derive macro](https://docs.rs/derive.CheckBytes.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#layout-stability)Layout stability

The layouts of types may change between compiler versions, or even different
compilations. To guarantee stable type layout between compilations, structs,
enums, and unions can be annotated with `#[repr(C)]`, and enums specifically
can be annotated with `#[repr(int)]` or `#[repr(C, int)]` as well. See
[the reference’s page on type layout](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/type-layout.html) for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `derive`: Re-exports the macros from- `bytecheck_derive`. Enabled by default.
- `simdutf8`: Uses the- `simdutf8`crate to validate UTF-8 strings. Enabled by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#crates)Crates

Bytecheck provides integrations for some common crates by default. In the future, crates should depend on bytecheck and provide their own integration.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use bytecheck::{CheckBytes, check_bytes, rancor::Failure};
#[derive(CheckBytes, Debug)]
#[repr(C)]
struct Test {
    a: u32,
    b: char,
    c: bool,
}
#[repr(C, align(4))]
struct Aligned<const N: usize>([u8; N]);
macro_rules! bytes {
    ($($byte:literal,)*) => {
        (&Aligned([$($byte,)*]).0 as &[u8]).as_ptr()
    };
    ($($byte:literal),*) => {
        bytes!($($byte,)*)
    };
}
// In this example, the architecture is assumed to be little-endian
#[cfg(target_endian = "little")]
unsafe {
    // These are valid bytes for a `Test`
    check_bytes::<Test, Failure>(
        bytes![
            0u8, 0u8, 0u8, 0u8,
            0x78u8, 0u8, 0u8, 0u8,
            1u8, 255u8, 255u8, 255u8,
        ].cast()
    ).unwrap();
    // Changing the bytes for the u32 is OK, any bytes are a valid u32
    check_bytes::<Test, Failure>(
        bytes![
            42u8, 16u8, 20u8, 3u8,
            0x78u8, 0u8, 0u8, 0u8,
            1u8, 255u8, 255u8, 255u8,
        ].cast()
    ).unwrap();
    // Characters outside the valid ranges are invalid
    check_bytes::<Test, Failure>(
        bytes![
            0u8, 0u8, 0u8, 0u8,
            0x00u8, 0xd8u8, 0u8, 0u8,
            1u8, 255u8, 255u8, 255u8,
        ].cast()
    ).unwrap_err();
    check_bytes::<Test, Failure>(
        bytes![
            0u8, 0u8, 0u8, 0u8,
            0x00u8, 0x00u8, 0x11u8, 0u8,
            1u8, 255u8, 255u8, 255u8,
        ].cast()
    ).unwrap_err();
    // 0 is a valid boolean value (false) but 2 is not
    check_bytes::<Test, Failure>(
        bytes![
            0u8, 0u8, 0u8, 0u8,
            0x78u8, 0u8, 0u8, 0u8,
            0u8, 255u8, 255u8, 255u8,
        ].cast()
    ).unwrap();
    check_bytes::<Test, Failure>(
        bytes![
            0u8, 0u8, 0u8, 0u8,
            0x78u8, 0u8, 0u8, 0u8,
            2u8, 255u8, 255u8, 255u8,
        ].cast()
    ).unwrap_err();
}
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [rancor](https://docs.rs/rancor/0.1.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rancor/index.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Invalid](https://docs.rs/struct.InvalidEnumDiscriminantError.html)- Enum - Discriminant - Error
- An error resulting from an invalid enum tag.
- [Named](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedEnumVariantCheckContext.html)- Enum - Variant - Check - Context
- Context for errors resulting from checking enum variants with named fields.
- [Struct](https://docs.rs/struct.StructCheckContext.html)- Check - Context
- Context for errors resulting from invalid structs.
- [Tuple](https://docs.rs/struct.TupleStructCheckContext.html)- Struct - Check - Context
- Context for errors resulting from invalid tuple structs.
- [Unnamed](https://docs.rs/struct.UnnamedEnumVariantCheckContext.html)- Enum - Variant - Check - Context
- Context for errors resulting from checking enum variants with unnamed fields.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- A type that can check whether a pointer points to a valid value.
- [Verify](https://docs.rs/trait.Verify.html)
- A type that can check whether its invariants are upheld.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- Checks whether the given pointer points to a valid value.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_bytes_with_context.html)- bytes_ - with_ - context - ⚠

# bytes - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytes/^1/

## Expand description

Provides abstractions for working with bytes.

The `bytes` crate provides an efficient byte buffer structure
([ Bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Bytes.html)) and traits for working with buffer
implementations (

[,](https://docs.rs/buf/trait.Buf.html)

`Buf`[).](https://docs.rs/buf/trait.BufMut.html)

`BufMut`[§](https://docs.rs#bytes)`Bytes`

`Bytes` is an efficient container for storing and operating on contiguous
slices of memory. It is intended for use primarily in networking code, but
could have applications elsewhere as well.

`Bytes` values facilitate zero-copy network programming by allowing multiple
`Bytes` objects to point to the same underlying memory. This is managed by
using a reference count to track when the memory is no longer needed and can
be freed.

A `Bytes` handle can be created directly from an existing byte store (such as `&[u8]`
or `Vec<u8>`), but usually a `BytesMut` is used first and written to. For
example:

```
use bytes::{BytesMut, BufMut};
let mut buf = BytesMut::with_capacity(1024);
buf.put(&b"hello world"[..]);
buf.put_u16(1234);
let a = buf.split();
assert_eq!(a, b"hello world\x04\xD2"[..]);
buf.put(&b"goodbye world"[..]);
let b = buf.split();
assert_eq!(b, b"goodbye world"[..]);
assert_eq!(buf.capacity(), 998);
```
In the above example, only a single buffer of 1024 is allocated. The handles
`a` and `b` will share the underlying buffer and maintain indices tracking
the view into the buffer represented by the handle.

See the [struct docs](https://docs.rs/struct.Bytes.html) for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#buf-bufmut)`Buf`, `BufMut`

These two traits provide read and write access to buffers. The underlying
storage may or may not be in contiguous memory. For example, `Bytes` is a
buffer that guarantees contiguous memory, but a [rope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rope_(data_structure)) stores the bytes in
disjoint chunks. `Buf` and `BufMut` maintain cursors tracking the current
position in the underlying byte storage. When bytes are read or written, the
cursor is advanced.

[§](https://docs.rs#relation-with-read-and-write)Relation with `Read` and `Write`

At first glance, it may seem that `Buf` and `BufMut` overlap in
functionality with [ std::io::Read](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Read.html) and

[. However, they serve different purposes. A buffer is the value that is provided as an argument to](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html)

`std::io::Write``Read::read` and `Write::write`. `Read` and `Write` may then
perform a syscall, which has the potential of failing. Operations on `Buf`
and `BufMut` are infallible.## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buf](https://docs.rs/buf/index.html)
- Utilities for working with buffers.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Bytes.html)
- A cheaply cloneable and sliceable chunk of contiguous memory.
- [Bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.BytesMut.html)- Mut
- A unique reference to a contiguous slice of memory.
- [TryGet](https://docs.rs/struct.TryGetError.html)- Error
- Error type for the `try_get_`methods of`Buf``Buf``try_get_`methods.

---

# hashbrown - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hashbrown/^0.17/

## Expand description

This crate is a Rust port of Google’s high-performance [SwissTable](https://abseil.io/blog/20180927-swisstables) hash
map, adapted to make it a drop-in replacement for Rust’s standard `HashMap`
and `HashSet` types.

The original C++ version of [SwissTable](https://abseil.io/blog/20180927-swisstables) can be found [here](https://github.com/abseil/abseil-cpp/blob/master/absl/container/internal/raw_hash_set.h), and this
[CppCon talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncHmEUmJZf4) gives an overview of how the algorithm works.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [hash_](https://docs.rs/hash_map/index.html)- map
- A hash map implemented with quadratic probing and SIMD lookup.
- [hash_](https://docs.rs/hash_set/index.html)- set
- A hash set implemented as a `HashMap`where the value is`()`.
- [hash_](https://docs.rs/hash_table/index.html)- table
- A hash table implemented with quadratic probing and SIMD lookup.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Default](https://docs.rs/struct.DefaultHashBuilder.html)- Hash - Builder
- Default hash builder for the `S`type parameter of`HashMap``HashSet`
- [Default](https://docs.rs/struct.DefaultHasher.html)- Hasher
- Default hasher for `HashMap``HashSet`
- [HashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.HashMap.html)
- A hash map implemented with quadratic probing and SIMD lookup.
- [HashSet](https://docs.rs/struct.HashSet.html)
- A hash set implemented as a `HashMap`where the value is`()`.
- [Hash](https://docs.rs/struct.HashTable.html)- Table
- Low-level hash table with explicit hashing.

# indexmap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/indexmap/^2/

## Expand description

[ IndexMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.IndexMap.html) is a hash table where the iteration order of the key-value
pairs is independent of the hash values of the keys.

[ IndexSet](https://docs.rs/set/struct.IndexSet.html) is a corresponding hash set using the same implementation and
with similar properties.

[§](https://docs.rs#highlights)Highlights

[ IndexMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.IndexMap.html) and

[are drop-in compatible with the std](https://docs.rs/set/struct.IndexSet.html)

`IndexSet``HashMap`
and `HashSet`, but they also have some features of note:- The ordering semantics (see their documentation for details)
- Sorting methods and the `.pop()`
- The `Equivalent`
- The `MutableKeys``MutableValues`

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

To reduce the amount of compiled code in the crate by default, certain
features are gated behind [feature flags](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section). These allow you to opt in to (or
out of) functionality. Below is a list of the features available in this
crate.

- `std`: Enables features which require the Rust standard library. For more information see the section on- `no_std`
- `rayon`: Enables parallel iteration and other parallel methods.
- `serde`: Adds implementations for- `Serialize`- `Deserialize`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`- `IndexMap`- `map::serde_seq`
- `arbitrary`: Adds implementations for the- `arbitrary::Arbitrary`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`
- `quickcheck`: Adds implementations for the- `quickcheck::Arbitrary`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`
- `borsh`(- **deprecated**): Adds implementations for- `BorshSerialize`- `BorshDeserialize`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`- `borsh`- `indexmap`,- `borsh v1.5.6`added an- `indexmap`feature that should be used instead of enabling the feature here.

*Note: only the  std feature is enabled by default.*

[§](https://docs.rs#alternate-hashers)Alternate Hashers

[ IndexMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.IndexMap.html) and

[have a default hasher type](https://docs.rs/set/struct.IndexSet.html)

`IndexSet`[, just like the standard](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/hash/random/struct.RandomState.html)

`S = RandomState``HashMap` and `HashSet`, which is resistant to
HashDoS attacks but not the most performant. Type aliases can make it easier
to use alternate hashers:```
use fnv::FnvBuildHasher;
use indexmap::{IndexMap, IndexSet};
type FnvIndexMap<K, V> = IndexMap<K, V, FnvBuildHasher>;
type FnvIndexSet<T> = IndexSet<T, FnvBuildHasher>;
let std: IndexSet<i32> = (0..100).collect();
let fnv: FnvIndexSet<i32> = (0..100).collect();
assert_eq!(std, fnv);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rust-version)Rust Version

This version of indexmap requires Rust 1.85 or later.

The indexmap 2.x release series will use a carefully considered version upgrade policy, where in a later 2.x version, we will raise the minimum required Rust version.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-standard-library-targets)No Standard Library Targets

This crate supports being built without `std`, requiring `alloc` instead.
This is chosen by disabling the default “std” cargo feature, by adding
`default-features = false` to your dependency specification.

- Creating maps and sets using `new``with_capacity``std`. Use methods`IndexMap::default``with_hasher``with_capacity_and_hasher``twox-hash`.
- Macros `indexmap!``indexset!``std`. Use the macros`indexmap_with_default!``indexset_with_default!`

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [map](https://docs.rs/map/index.html)
- `IndexMap`
- [set](https://docs.rs/set/index.html)
- A hash set implemented using `IndexMap`

# munge - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/munge/^0.4/

## Expand description

Munge makes it easy and safe to destructure `MaybeUninit`s, `Cell`s,
`UnsafeCell`s, `ManuallyDrop`s and more.

Just use the `munge!` macro to destructure opaque types the same way you’d
destructure a value. The `munge!` macro may be used to perform either borrow
destructuring (e.g. `let (a, b) = c` where `c` is a reference) or move
destructuring (e.g. `let (a, b) = c` where `c` is a value) depending on the
type.

Munge has no features and is always `#![no_std]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Initialize `MaybeUninit`s:

```
use core::mem::MaybeUninit;
use munge::munge;
pub struct Example {
    a: u32,
    b: (char, f32),
}
let mut mu = MaybeUninit::<Example>::uninit();
munge!(let Example { a, b: (c, mut f) } = &mut mu);
assert_eq!(a.write(10), &10);
assert_eq!(c.write('x'), &'x');
assert_eq!(f.write(3.14), &3.14);
// Note that `mut` bindings can be reassigned like you'd expect:
f = &mut MaybeUninit::uninit();
// SAFETY: `mu` is completely initialized.
let init = unsafe { mu.assume_init() };
assert_eq!(init.a, 10);
assert_eq!(init.b.0, 'x');
assert_eq!(init.b.1, 3.14);
```
Destructure `Cell`s:

```
use core::cell::Cell;
use munge::munge;
pub struct Example {
    a: u32,
    b: (char, f32),
}
let value = Example {
    a: 10,
    b: ('x', 3.14),
};
let cell = Cell::<Example>::new(value);
munge!(let Example { a, b: (c, f) } = &cell);
assert_eq!(a.get(), 10);
a.set(42);
assert_eq!(c.get(), 'x');
c.set('!');
assert_eq!(f.get(), 3.14);
f.set(1.41);
let value = cell.into_inner();
assert_eq!(value.a, 42);
assert_eq!(value.b.0, '!');
assert_eq!(value.b.1, 1.41);
```
You can even extend munge to work with your own types by implementing its
`Destructure` and `Restructure` traits:

```
use munge::{Destructure, Restructure, Move, munge};
pub struct Invariant<T>(T);
impl<T> Invariant<T> {
    /// # Safety
    ///
    /// `value` must uphold my custom invariant.
    pub unsafe fn new_unchecked(value: T) -> Self {
        Self(value)
    }
    pub fn unwrap(self) -> T {
        self.0
    }
}
// SAFETY:
// - `Invariant<T>` is destructured by move, so its `Destructuring` type is
//   `Move`.
// - `underlying` returns a pointer to its inner type, so it is guaranteed
//   to be non-null, properly aligned, and valid for reads.
unsafe impl<T> Destructure for Invariant<T> {
    type Underlying = T;
    type Destructuring = Move;
    fn underlying(&mut self) -> *mut Self::Underlying {
        &mut self.0 as *mut Self::Underlying
    }
}
// SAFETY: `restructure` returns an `Invariant<U>` that takes ownership of
// the restructured field because `Invariant<T>` is destructured by move.
unsafe impl<T, U> Restructure<U> for Invariant<T> {
    type Restructured = Invariant<U>;
    unsafe fn restructure(&self, ptr: *mut U) -> Self::Restructured {
        // SAFETY: The caller has guaranteed that `ptr` is a pointer to a
        // subfield of some `T`, so it must be properly aligned, valid for
        // reads, and initialized. We may move the fields because the
        // destructuring type for `Invariant<T>` is `Move`.
        let value = unsafe { ptr.read() };
        Invariant(value)
    }
}
// SAFETY: `(1, 2, 3)` upholds my custom invariant.
let value = unsafe { Invariant::new_unchecked((1, 2, 3)) };
munge!(let (one, two, three) = value);
assert_eq!(one.unwrap(), 1);
assert_eq!(two.unwrap(), 2);
assert_eq!(three.unwrap(), 3);
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [munge](https://docs.rs/macro.munge.html)
- Destructures a type using a pattern.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Borrow](https://docs.rs/struct.Borrow.html)
- Destructuring by borrow, e.g. `let (a, b) = c`where`c`is a reference.
- [Move](https://docs.rs/struct.Move.html)
- Destructuring by move, e.g. `let (a, b) = c`where`c`is a value.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Destructure](https://docs.rs/trait.Destructure.html)
- A type that can be destructured into its constituent parts.
- [Restructure](https://docs.rs/trait.Restructure.html)
- A type that can be “restructured” as a field of some containing type.

# ptr_meta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ptr_meta/^0.3/

## Expand description

A radioactive stabilization of the [ ptr_meta RFC](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2580-ptr-meta.html).

This crate provides the [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) trait,

[and](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html)

`from_raw_parts`[functions, and proc macros for deriving](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html)

`to_raw_parts``Pointee` for
structs and implementing `Pointee` for trait objects.[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Raw pointers can be decomposed into the data address and metadata components
with [ to_raw_parts](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html) or

[.](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts_mut.html)

`to_raw_parts_mut`Alternatively, metadata alone can be extracted with the [ metadata](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)
function. Although

[accepts pointers, references can be passed and will be implicitly coerced.](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)

`metadata`A pointer can be created from its address and metadata with
[ from_raw_parts](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html) or

[.](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts_mut.html)

`from_raw_parts_mut`[§](https://docs.rs#provided-impls)Provided impls

`ptr_meta` provides inherent implementations for many builtin types:

- All `Sized``Pointee`
- `slice`,- `str`, and- `CStr`
- `OsStr`(requires- `std`)
- `dyn Any`, optionally with- `+ Send`and/or- `+ Sync`
- `dyn Error`, optionally with- `+ Send`and/or- `+ Sync`

[§](https://docs.rs#structs-with-trailing-dsts)Structs with trailing DSTs

You can derive [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) for structs with trailing DSTs:

```
use ptr_meta::Pointee;
#[derive(Pointee)]
struct Block<H, T> {
    header: H,
    elements: [T],
}
```
Note that the last field is required to be a DST. Structs with a generic
type as the last field may have conflicting blanket implementations, as the
generic type may be `Sized`. A collection of specific implementations may be
required in these cases, with the generic parameter set (for example) a
slice, `str`, or specific trait object.

[§](https://docs.rs#trait-objects)Trait objects

You can generate [ Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html) implementations for trait objects:

```
use ptr_meta::pointee;
// Generates Pointee for dyn Stringy
#[ptr_meta::pointee]
trait Stringy {
    fn as_string(&self) -> String;
}
```
Note that this will not produce implementations for `Trait + Send + Sync`.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `derive`: Re-exports the macros from- `ptr_meta_derive`. Enabled by default.
- `std`: Enables additional impls for- `std`types. Enabled by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
// Get the associated metadata for pointers
let str = "hello world";
assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata(str), str.len());
let slice = &[1, 2, 3, 4, 5] as &[i32];
assert_eq!(ptr_meta::metadata(slice), slice.len());
// Make your own wide pointers from data pointers and metadata
let bytes = [b'h', b'e', b'l', b'l', b'o'];
let ptr = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<str>(bytes.as_ptr().cast(), 5);
println!("{} world!", unsafe { &*ptr }); // prints "hello world!"
// Derive Pointee on your own types
#[derive(ptr_meta::Pointee)]
#[repr(transparent)]
struct CoolStr {
    inner: str,
}
impl CoolStr {
    fn print_cool(&self) {
        println!("😎 {} 😎", &self.inner);
    }
}
let ptr = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<CoolStr>(bytes.as_ptr().cast(), 5);
let cool = unsafe { &*ptr };
cool.print_cool(); // prints "😎 hello 😎"
// Implement Pointee for trait objects
#[ptr_meta::pointee]
trait Printable {
    fn print(&self);
}
impl Printable for i32 {
    fn print(&self) {
        println!("i32: {self}");
    }
}
let i32_vtable = ptr_meta::metadata(&0i32 as &dyn Printable);
let one_hundred = 100i32;
let printable = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts::<dyn Printable>(
    (&one_hundred as *const i32).cast(),
    i32_vtable,
);
unsafe {
    (*printable).print(); // prints "i32: 100"
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [DynMetadata](https://docs.rs/struct.DynMetadata.html)
- The metadata for a trait object.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Pointee](https://docs.rs/trait.Pointee.html)
- A trait which associates pointer metadata with a pointee type.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts.html)- raw_ - parts
- Returns a raw pointer with the given data address and metadata.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_raw_parts_mut.html)- raw_ - parts_ - mut
- Returns a mutable raw pointer with the given data address and metadata.
- [metadata](https://docs.rs/fn.metadata.html)
- Returns the metadata of the given pointer.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts.html)- raw_ - parts
- Returns the data address and metadata of the given pointer.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_raw_parts_mut.html)- raw_ - parts_ - mut
- Returns the mutable data address and metadata of the given pointer.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [pointee](https://docs.rs/attr.pointee.html)- `derive`
- Generates a `Pointee`implementation for trait object of the labeled trait.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Pointee](https://docs.rs/derive.Pointee.html)- `derive`
- Derives `Pointee`for the labeled struct which has a trailing DST.

# rancor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rancor/^0.1/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rancor)rancor

rancor provides scalable and efficient error handling without using type composition. This makes it best-suited for situations where:

- Programmatic error introspection is not useful
- Functions may error, but succeed most of the time
- Errors should provide as much useful detail as possible when emitted
- Use cases include both `no_std`and targets with support for`std`

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `alloc`: Provides the- `BoxedError`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [fail](https://docs.rs/macro.fail.html)
- Returns the given error from this function.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Boxed](https://docs.rs/struct.BoxedError.html)- Error - `alloc`
- An error type that preserves all detailed error messages. It is optimized to fit in a single pointer.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- A good general-purpose error type.
- [Failure](https://docs.rs/struct.Failure.html)
- An error type that only preserves success or failure, throwing away any more detailed error messages.
- [Strategy](https://docs.rs/struct.Strategy.html)
- Equips a type with a `Fallible`implementation that chooses`E`as its error type.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Infallible](https://docs.rs/enum.Infallible.html)
- A re-export of `core::convert::Infallible`. The error type for errors that can never happen.
- [Panic](https://docs.rs/enum.Panic.html)
- An error type that does not occupy any space, panicking on creation instead.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Fallible](https://docs.rs/trait.Fallible.html)
- A type with fallible operations that return its associated error type.
- [Never](https://docs.rs/trait.Never.html)
- A type that can never be produced.
- [Option](https://docs.rs/trait.OptionExt.html)- Ext
- Helper methods for `Option`s.
- [Result](https://docs.rs/trait.ResultExt.html)- Ext
- Helper methods for `Result`s.
- [Source](https://docs.rs/trait.Source.html)
- An error type which can be uniformly constructed from an `Error`
- [Trace](https://docs.rs/trait.Trace.html)
- An error type which can add additional “trace” information to itself.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [unreachable_](https://docs.rs/fn.unreachable_checked.html)- checked
- Consumes a `Never`type, returning a primitive`!`.

---

# rend - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rend/^0.5/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rend)rend

rend provides cross-platform, endian-aware primitives for Rust.

rend does not provide cross-platform alternatives for types that are
inherently cross-platform, such as `bool` and `u8`. It also does not provide
cross-platform alternatives for types that have an architecture-dependent
size, such as `isize` and `usize`. rend does not support custom types.

rend is intended to be used to build portable types that can be shared between different architectures.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `bytecheck`: Enables support for validating types using- `bytecheck`.

[§](https://docs.rs#crates)Crates

- `zerocopy-0_8`

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example:

```
use core::mem::transmute;
use rend::*;
let little_int = i32_le::from_native(0x12345678);
// Internal representation is little-endian
assert_eq!(
    [0x78, 0x56, 0x34, 0x12],
    unsafe { transmute::<_, [u8; 4]>(little_int) }
);
// Can also be made with `.into()`
let little_int: i32_le = 0x12345678.into();
// Still formats correctly
assert_eq!("305419896", format!("{}", little_int));
assert_eq!("0x12345678", format!("0x{:x}", little_int));
let big_int = i32_be::from_native(0x12345678);
// Internal representation is big-endian
assert_eq!(
    [0x12, 0x34, 0x56, 0x78],
    unsafe { transmute::<_, [u8; 4]>(big_int) }
);
// Can also be made with `.into()`
let big_int: i32_be = 0x12345678.into();
// Still formats correctly
assert_eq!("305419896", format!("{}", big_int));
assert_eq!("0x12345678", format!("0x{:x}", big_int));
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [unaligned](https://docs.rs/unaligned/index.html)
- Cross-platform primitives with unaligned representations.

Source: https://docs.rs/smallvec/^1/

docs.rs failed to build smallvec-1.15.2

Please check the

See

If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

Please check the

[build logs](https://docs.rs/crate/smallvec/1.15.2/builds)for more information.See

[Builds](https://docs.rs/about/builds)for ideas on how to fix a failed build, or[Metadata](https://docs.rs/about/metadata)for how to configure docs.rs builds.If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).# rust-smallvec

"Small vector" optimization for Rust: store up to a small number of items on the stack

## Example

```
use ;

// This SmallVec can hold up to 4 items on the stack:
let mut v:  = smallvec!;
// It will automatically move its contents to the heap if
// contains more than four items:
v.push;
// SmallVec points to a slice, so you can use normal slice
// indexing and other methods to access its contents:
v = v + v;
v.sort;
```
